﻿# Asset registry — Viaduct facility (excerpt)

The registry is the index of assets at the Viaduct facility. It answers one question: which asset am I
looking at, and what is its identifier? Recorded values are deliberately excluded — each row names the
document where the value is held, so that a value has exactly one home and correcting it does not require
correcting an index.

The excerpt below covers the cooling and air-handling assets of the north half of the facility. The full
registry, including the low-voltage distribution and the roof plant, lives in the same series with a
different suffix and is reissued whenever an asset is added or retired.

## Cooling assets

| Asset | Description | Value held in |
|---|---|---|
| NBL-420 | West-aisle cooling loop | limit schedule |
| NBL-118 | East-aisle cooling loop | limit schedule |

## Air handling assets

A transferred asset that has not yet been re-measured is marked in the ticket system but not in this
register, which is a known gap: the register has no status column. The gap is recorded here so that a reader
who notices an unexpectedly early value knows why it looks that way.

## Revision history

- 2025.12 — three distribution boards added; one retired identifier removed.
- 2025.09 — two transferred assets re-recorded at transfer values.
- 2025.05 — separator convention aligned with the Viaduct series.

## Scope

This document records values. It does not describe assets, and a reader who needs a description should use
the Rosario registry rather than infer one from an identifier. It also does not record inspection grades,
which live with the inspection reports and are revised on a different schedule.

## Custody

The register is maintained by the Rosario calibration team and reviewed when the Viaduct series is revised,
so that the two files do not drift in convention even though they are never merged. Where the two disagree
about a convention rather than a value, the disagreement is resolved by the facilities lead for the estate
and recorded in both revision histories.

# Recorded value register — Rosario facility

Revision 2025.12. This register covers the Rosario facility only. It is issued as a separate series from the
Viaduct register and the two must not be merged: identifiers are unique within a facility, not across the
estate, and a merged file has produced two transposed readings in the past.

Two assets were transferred to Rosario from the Viaduct facility when the southern hall was consolidated.
Both kept their Viaduct identifiers and both were re-recorded here at the value they carried at transfer,
because the calibration team re-measures an asset after a move rather than assuming the value survives it.

A correction to a description is a registry change and is reviewed by the facilities lead. A correction to a
recorded value is not: values live in the register, and their correction is a register change. Keeping those
two paths separate is why the index can be read quickly during an incident without anyone needing to check
whether the value beside an identifier is current.

## What the registry is not

It is not a maintenance history, a warranty list or a commissioning record. Those documents exist, they cite
identifiers from this registry, and they are not substitutes for it. A ticket that describes an asset without
its identifier is treated as incomplete at the change review, which is the reason the registry is short
enough to be read aloud.

supersession rather than overwriting the row.

# Retention and evidence policy

## Purpose

This policy fixes how long operational records are kept and what counts as evidence when a decision is
challenged later. It exists because the estate has twice been asked to justify a change that nobody could
reconstruct from memory.

## What is retained

Change tickets, incident timelines and their attachments are retained for seven years. Badge logs are
retained for two years, with the exception of entries linked to an incident, which inherit the incident's
retention period. Audit packs — the signed checklist, the photographs and the reviewer's note — are retained

Recorded values published in registers are retained for the life of the asset plus three years, because a
decommissioned asset can still be the subject of a warranty claim long after the physical unit is gone.

## What is not retained

# Change-control checklist — platform facilities

Applies to every change raised against the facility estate, including work carried out by vendors under
a framework agreement. The checklist is filled in by the change raiser and countersigned by the shift
supervisor before the ticket leaves draft.

## Before the change

- [ ] A change record exists with a single named owner, a start and end window, and a rollback step written
      by someone other than the person who will execute it.
- [ ] The rollback step names the exact state to restore and the person who verifies it afterwards.
- [ ] Any safety interlock that must be bypassed is listed, together with the mitigation that replaces it
      while the bypass is active.
- [ ] The affected room and rack are named. "Facilities" is not an acceptable location.
- [ ] A second engineer has read the plan and signed it. For changes that touch power distribution the
      reviewer must be from the electrical team.

## During the change

## Notes

Entries are revised when an asset is re-measured by the facilities group, and a re-measurement that confirms
an existing entry is still entered as a revision. Superseded entries are struck rather than deleted, so a
ticket that quotes an older entry can still be reconciled against the schedule.

Identifiers are never reused. Where a replacement asset occupies the position of a retired one, the
replacement receives a new identifier and both appear in the schedule for one revision before the retired row
is struck.

Separators are transcribed by hand as often as they are copied. A line with the wrong number of separators is
rejected by the ticket validator before a work order is issued, which is the cheapest place for that defect
to be caught.

Handovers are written, not spoken. A spoken handover reaches the next shift and nobody else; a written one
reaches the engineer who is called at three in the morning two weeks later and needs to know why a circuit
was left isolated.

## Standing notes

The plant rooms are visited on a walking round twice per shift. Round times are recorded, because a round
that is consistently recorded at the same minute is a round that is being signed off from the office. The
security lead samples the timestamps monthly and has, on two occasions, asked for the round to be repeated
under observation.

Rooms under construction are excluded from the round only while the contractor's permit is open, and the
exclusion ends automatically when the permit expires. An exclusion that outlives its permit is treated as a
finding in the next audit.

## Access notes

erection, and the resulting delay is billed. The corridor also carries a services tray at head height that
must be isolated before the scaffold is placed; the isolation is a change of its own and is raised with the
normal change process.

fault is traced to a loop, the loop's record is updated rather than this one, so that a reader who starts
from the loop reaches the loop's evidence and not an inspection note that mentions it in passing.

The walkthrough audit is now run every six weeks. The previous semi-annual cadence was set when the
estate held two halls; with seven halls in scope a semi-annual pass meant that a hall could go five months

same tray produced descriptions that could not be compared.

## Structure of a note

The first paragraph says what customers can observe, in their terms. The second says what is being done and
by whom. The third, when known, says when the next update will follow. Anything else — hypotheses, internal
tooling names, the names of engineers — is left out of the customer-facing note and recorded in the internal
timeline instead.

Internal notes carry more detail. They name the working theory, the person testing it, and the two or three
diagnostics already excluded. An internal note that lists every alarm without saying which ones were ruled
out costs the next responder the same investigation twice.

## Postmortem

A postmortem is written for every S1 and for any S2 that repeated within the quarter. It is blameless in the
narrow sense that it names systems and decisions rather than individuals, and it ends with no more than
three actions, each with an owner and a date. Postmortems with ten actions are treated as having none: the
review samples whether the actions were completed, and a list nobody finishes scores worse than a short one
that closes.

explicitly: a re-measurement that confirms the existing value is still a re-measurement and is recorded as

because the return temperature had not settled at the three-hour mark, which the commissioning engineer
recorded as an observation rather than a finding: the loop settled inside the tolerance during the
additional hour and held for the remainder.

not from the design figure in the specification, and the two differ by a small margin that the commissioning

## Deviations

Three deviations were recorded during commissioning. Two were closed on the day. The third — a missing

days later. The punch item is referenced in the handover pack, and the label is present in the as-built
drawing revision that followed.

The loop was not de-rated. Where a commissioning measurement falls outside the design tolerance the
commissioning engineer can either de-rate the asset or accept it with a written rationale; in this case the
measurement fell inside the tolerance once the soak was extended, so neither was required.

## Operating envelope

The loop runs at a fixed supply temperature with a modulating secondary pump. Operators are not expected to
adjust the set point; where a room reports discomfort the response is to check the air-handling unit serving
that room before touching the loop, because in practice the loop is adjusted four or five times for every
genuine air-handling fault.

that a reader who starts from the asset can reach the evidence in one step. Project files are archived after

The second re-measurement followed a leak on the shared manifold, which was repaired without affecting the
loop's measurement.

## Method

Readings are taken with the loop at steady state, which the team defines as three consecutive samples inside
a two-percent band. Sampling before steady state is the most common source of spurious drift reports, and it
is the first thing the calibration team checks when an operator reports a value that "moved overnight".

Two engineers take the reading independently when the value is being revised. Where their readings differ by
more than the tolerance, both are recorded and the asset is scheduled for a third reading rather than
averaging the two, because an average of two disagreeing measurements hides whichever one is wrong.

The shared manifold remains on the watch list. It has been flagged twice in three quarters, both times for
the same reason: the isolation valves on the eastern side do not fully seat, so a service on one loop bleeds
pressure from the other. The valves are on the maintenance backlog with a date and an owner, and until they
are replaced the two loops are scheduled apart.

Applies to every change raised against the facility estate, including work carried out by vendors under
a framework agreement. The checklist is filled in by the change raiser and countersigned by the shift
supervisor before the ticket leaves draft.

- [ ] Any safety interlock that must be bypassed is listed, together with the mitigation that replaces it

- [ ] The affected room and rack are named. "Facilities" is not an acceptable location.
- [ ] A second engineer has read the plan and signed it. For changes that touch power distribution the
      reviewer must be from the electrical team.

## During the change

Visitors sign a printed register on arrival and departure. The register exists because badge logs alone
cannot distinguish a visitor who left with their escort from a visitor who left alone an hour later, which
is the question the security lead asks first after any incident.

## 3.3 Keys and cabinets

Physical keys are held in the cabinet beside the north corridor entrance and signed out individually.
Cabinet keys are numbered; a missing key freezes every lock in its group until the cylinder is replaced,
which is deliberately more expensive than the alternative of keeping a spare under a desk.

## 3.4 Reviews and revocation

Access is reviewed quarterly against the current staffing list. Leavers are removed on their last working
day by the same step that closes their payroll record, so the two lists cannot drift apart. Anyone returning
from more than eight weeks of leave is re-reviewed before their badge is reactivated, because a role can
change while a badge is dormant.

## Forecast

The forecast assumes the batch window does not widen. If the reconciliation jobs move into the working day,
the peak shifts rather than grows and the flags above become more urgent than their numbers suggest. The
forecast is revised after the mid-quarter checkpoint, and the revision is published as a new version of
this memo rather than as an appended paragraph, so a reader always knows which version they are holding.

- Rebalance the batch schedule so that backup and reconciliation do not overlap. Owner: data platform.
- Order one spare unit for the hall flagged on headroom. Owner: procurement, with facilities confirming the
  physical space before the order is placed.
- Re-run the ratio calculation after the rebalance and publish the result with the next review.

does not authorise work on a hall. Those decisions belong to the change process and are recorded there.

## Method note

AHU-233 recorded an inspection grade of one, with no notes. The recorded value for AHU-233 is NBR-5F2D-3094,
likewise unchanged.

## Grades

The inspection grade is not a quality score for the unit; it describes the amount of follow-up the
inspection generated. Grade one means no follow-up, grade two means a note for the next cycle, grade three
means an action with an owner and a date. An inspector who issues a grade three for a cosmetic defect is
asked to justify it, because grades three consumes maintenance capacity that the backlog would otherwise
spend on a fault.

## Filters

Filter changes are recorded separately from inspections and are not part of the grade. The two units are on
the same filter schedule, which is why they are inspected together: a schedule that treats them separately
tends to produce two half-loads of filters and a storeroom that is out of the size that is actually needed.
